metadata.title: Educational improvement through machine learning: Strategic models for better PISA scores

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 data for 37 OECD countries and constructs categorical predictors (e.g., ESCS, ICTRES, metacognition, weekly instruction hours) to build Random Forest models for reading, mathematics, and science. The manuscript states that there was no missing data and describes extensive preprocessing (categorization, removal of insignificant variables, and thresholding countries using OECD-average cut points), but it does not report any use of PISA sampling weights or replicate weights. Because the analysis is implemented in R using Random Forest via the Boruta package, the paper does not document whether complex survey design weights were applied; therefore, weighting strategy cannot be verified from the provided text. Analysts using the PISA international database should apply the official student sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) when estimating country-representative relationships, especially given the nested sampling structure (students within schools within countries).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are described as “standardised PISA scores” for science, mathematics, and reading, but the paper does not specify whether these are PV-based achievement scores (as in PISA) and how PVs were handled in the Random Forest classification/regression pipeline. The manuscript also claims “there was no missing data,” yet it does not document how missingness was assessed (e.g., item nonresponse vs. variable-level missingness) or what was done if any missing values existed after recoding/categorization. This combination creates a reporting gap: PV handling and missing-data treatment are essential for reproducibility with PISA microdata.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 data for 37 OECD countries and focused on three achievement domains (science, reading, mathematics). Countries were categorized as high-performing vs low-performing using OECD-average thresholds (reading >487, maths >489, science >489). The study then built domain-specific Random Forest models using 24 categorical predictors (student and contextual variables) after converting continuous variables into categories, removing insignificant variables, and applying Boruta feature selection. The manuscript states that there was no missing data.

main_findings.target_variable: Reading success (high vs low using OECD-average threshold)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest with Boruta feature selection. Reported variable coefficient estimates: CPERWEEK=0.844 (highest), ICTRES=0.124, METASPAM=0.124, ESCS=0.263, HISEI=0.406, CPERFORLAN=0.815. Success threshold from model: predicted score >3.219 for reading.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (OECD countries) reading the study leveraged ICT access (ICTRES), foreign language lessons per week (CPERFORLAN), total weekly teaching load (CPERWEEK), metacognition (METASPAM), and ESCS/HISEI to predict reading success (high vs low using OECD-average thresholds), finding that CPERWEEK and CPERFORLAN have the strongest positive contributions while METASPAM and ICTRES have smaller coefficients. This indicates that strengthening instructional time allocation and foreign-language instruction may be a practical lever for improving reading performance in high-performing OECD contexts, though the paper does not document PV handling or survey-weighted estimation.

main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics success (high vs low using OECD-average threshold)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest with Boruta feature selection. Reported variable coefficient estimates: COMPETE=0.628 (highest), HISEI=0.412, METASPAM=0.291, ESCS=0.188, ICTRES=0.174, CPERWEEK=0.073 (lowest). Success threshold from model: predicted score >2.396 for mathematics.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (OECD countries) mathematics the study leveraged academic competition (COMPETE), parental occupational status (HISEI), metacognition (METASPAM), ESCS, and ICT access (ICTRES) to predict mathematics success (high vs low using OECD-average thresholds), finding that COMPETE is the strongest contributor and CPERWEEK is the weakest among the selected predictors. This indicates that policies fostering constructive competitive motivation and related classroom dynamics may align with higher mathematics performance, while simply increasing total weekly teaching load may not be sufficient, especially given the study’s limited reporting on PV and missing-data procedures.

main_findings.target_variable: Science success (high vs low using OECD-average threshold)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest with Boruta feature selection. Reported variable coefficient estimates: METASPAM=0.550 (highest), ICTRES=0.484, CPERWEEK=0.340, JOYREAD=0.219, ESCS=0.206, HISEI=0.285, COMPETE=0.029, PISADIFF=0.030. Success threshold from model: predicted score >2.732 for science.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (OECD countries) science the study leveraged metacognition (METASPAM), ICT access (ICTRES), total weekly teaching load (CPERWEEK), perceived PISA test difficulty (PISADIFF), and reading enjoyment (JOYREAD) to predict science success (high vs low using OECD-average thresholds), finding that metacognitive credibility judgment and ICT access have the largest positive contributions while perceived difficulty and competition have near-zero coefficients. This indicates that interventions targeting students’ metacognitive skills and effective digital access may be more aligned with science performance gains than focusing primarily on test-difficulty perceptions, though causality cannot be inferred and PV/weighting details are not provided.

data.outcome_summary: This PLOS One study uses PISA 2018 data for 37 OECD countries and builds Random Forest prediction models for domain-specific “success” in reading, mathematics, and science. Countries are dichotomized as high-performing vs low-performing using OECD-average cut points (reading >487, maths >489, science >489), and 24 categorical predictors are recoded and feature-selected with Boruta. The best-performing approach is Random Forest (no alternative ML models are reported), and the paper reports domain-specific coefficient estimates and model-derived success thresholds (reading >3.219; maths >2.396; science >2.732). The most consistently important predictors across domains include ICT access (ICTRES), weekly instructional load (CPERWEEK), and metacognition (METASPAM), with additional domain-specific factors such as foreign-language lessons for reading and academic competition for mathematics. Limitations include lack of documented plausible-value (PV) handling, unclear missing-data treatment beyond a claim of “no missing data,” and no reported survey-weight/replicate-weight strategy, so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
